title: Which problems should a family office COO hand to AI first?
description: A family office COO's problem list, ranked by hours: the quarterly report, fund documents, books, deadlines and manager diligence, with who signs off.
verdict: Start where the hours go: 73% of 155 family offices in the Americas call investment reporting too manual.[^5][^42]
Fund documents: 54% of advisors and alt investors spent 10+ hours weekly on them (2021).[^36] Each investment averages 13 yearly.[^37]
By our count, a model 30-filer office faces 159 federal, SEC and Delaware deadlines a year, peaking in autumn.[^16][^17]
Lacking diligence teams, 23% of investors assign it to the COO.[^38] 39% of offices use or seek AI for it.[^39]
AI drafts, extracts and flags, while a named person approves every payment, filing, report and commitment.[^1][^8]

answers.human-role: Your people keep every payment, filing, investment call and family report, while AI drafts, extracts and flags work for them to check.[^1][^8]
answers.decisions: A family office COO owns six AI calls: what to fix first, what data goes in, who checks output, vendor features, buy or build, and how to measure.[^1][^9]
answers.ranked: The quarterly report and fund documents eat the most hours, then the books, the deadline calendar and manager diligence, as far as surveys measure them.[^5][^36][^41]
answers.faq: The principal or family will ask about data safety, savings so far, fraud, the SEC, what peers do and whether to hire.[^1][^3]
answers.recipes: A 90-day start is one job, four weeks of baseline hours, a six-week pilot on tools you already license, then a keep, change or stop call.[^6][^1]
answers.own-data: Our count found 159 federal, SEC and Delaware filing deadlines a year for a model 30-filer office, or about 3 every working week.[^16][^24]
answers.benchmark: Show it worked by timing two jobs for four weeks, piloting against a hold-out group, and pricing the hours saved in dollars.[^28][^12]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI in a family office goes wrong through spoofed payment requests, missing incident plans, stalled pilots, wrong facts sent to the family and single points of failure.[^8][^7]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy first, because most family offices prefer ready-made tools and 57% cite lack of internal expertise as the biggest barrier.[^1][^2]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when providers do most of the work, an operating business dominates, you are a registered adviser, or the pain is a multi-entity close.[^3][^15]

summary: AI changes how fast a family office COO's team clears paperwork: statements, notices, deadlines and drafts get a first pass.[^1][^3] The COO runs the office as an operating business: reporting, technology, compliance, vendors and controls.[^10] AI pays only with privacy controls and a named reviewer.[^1]
humanRole: COO: owns the list of approved AI tools, what family data may go in, and which outputs need a human check.[^1][^9]
Controller: reviews every AI-extracted capital call, K-1 figure or journal entry before it posts. Citi found careful offices treat AI output as drafts needing human checks.[^1]
Payment approver: a named person approves every wire and bank-detail change, with a call-back. FinCEN warns criminals use deepfakes of executives to order transfers.[^8]
Principal or chief investment officer: keeps every investment decision and fund commitment, and signs off what the family sees. Citi found final decisions stay with experienced people.[^1]

decisions.know: Where staff hours go today. Family office executives spend 19% of their time on administration and compliance, 27% in North America.[^6]

decisions.decision: What family data may go into AI
decisions.know: Citi calls privacy non-negotiable for family offices.[^1] In Citi's 2025 survey of 346 family offices, 28% cite cybersecurity or privacy as a barrier to new technology.[^2]

decisions.decision: Who checks output, and how closely
decisions.know: Careful offices fully review AI summaries first, then move to spot-checks as confidence builds.[^1] NIST, the US standards agency, asks for written human oversight roles.[^9]

decisions.decision: Which vendor AI features to switch on
decisions.know: Some offices already get AI through the back door, via software providers and devices they use.[^1] Read each provider's AI terms before a feature goes live.
Most family offices prefer to buy, and some build only for 80%+ efficiency gains.[^1] Lack of internal expertise is the top barrier, cited by 57% of family offices.[^1]
Only 18% of single-family offices in the Americas report AI cut operating costs, and 43% see no measurable impact.[^4] So time each job before the pilot starts.

ranked.name: The quarterly report
ranked.why: 73% of 155 family offices in the Americas say investment reporting is too manual, a top concern three years running.[^5] Citi found monthly adviser reports still merged into Excel by hand.[^1]
ranked.payoff: Days from month-end to the family's report, and breaks per cycle.

ranked.name: Fund documents: statements, calls, distributions and K-1 tax forms
ranked.why: In a 2021 vendor-run survey of 400+ advisors and alternative investors, 54% spent at least 10 hours a week managing alternatives documents.[^36] The average private markets investment sends 13 documents a year, by Arch's platform data.[^37]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per document from portal to filed, and documents still keyed by hand.

ranked.name: Capital calls and K-1s in the books
ranked.why: Citi found family office tax work highly manual and voluminous.[^1] In our model office, by our count, 15 trust and personal returns wait on 13 partnership K-1s.[^16][^17]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per document, and fields the controller corrects.

ranked.name: Bookkeeping, bill pay and entity accounting
ranked.why: Family offices spend 20% of working hours on manual tasks, up to 40% in larger offices, in a sponsored survey of 44 offices.[^41] Bill pay is the task family offices most often keep fully in-house, at 69%.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Days to close each entity, and invoices handled per person.

ranked.name: The filing and compliance calendar
ranked.why: By our count, a model 30-filer office faces 159 federal, SEC and Delaware deadlines a year.[^16][^24] Family office executives spend 19% of their time on administration and compliance.[^6]
ranked.payoff: Deadlines met without a scramble, and hours spent chasing documents.

ranked.name: Comparing fund managers before committing
ranked.why: 41% of 44 investors in an operational due diligence survey say they lack time to finish reviews.[^38] Where investors have no dedicated team, 23% put the work under the COO or operations.[^38]
ranked.payoff: Weeks from the first questionnaire to the committee memo, and answers checked against evidence.

ranked.name: Email, meeting notes and memos
ranked.why: Copilot users spent about 2 fewer hours a week on email in a field study of 7,137 workers.[^28] Writing tasks took 40% less time with ChatGPT in a controlled study.[^29]
ranked.payoff: Hours a week on email, notes and memos.

ranked.name: Software, vendors and security
ranked.why: Choosing new software can take 8 to 12 weeks and implementing it 3 to 6 months, per Deloitte.[^6] So a 90-day start runs on tools you already license.
ranked.payoff: Vendor AI terms read, and features switched on with sign-off.

faq.q: Is the family's data safe in these tools?
faq.a: Only on business plans with admin controls and a written rule on what data goes in.[^31][^1] Citi calls privacy non-negotiable.[^1] In Citi's 2025 survey, 28% of family offices cite cybersecurity or privacy as a barrier.[^2]

faq.q: What has AI saved other family offices so far?
faq.a: Little measured cost so far: only 18% of single-family offices in the Americas report AI cut operating costs.[^4] Another 29% of those offices say it is too early, so set a baseline before day one.[^4]

faq.q: Can AI vet a fund manager for us?
faq.a: No, not on its own: AI can line up a manager's questionnaire answers, but the investment committee decides.[^38][^40] The Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) says yes/no answers give only a top-level view, so follow up before deciding.[^40] 39% of 245 family offices in Goldman Sachs' survey use or look to use AI for investment due diligence and decision support.[^39]

faq.q: Are we exposed to AI-driven fraud?
faq.a: Yes: 72% of family offices in a Bank of America survey say the office or a family member has faced fraud.[^3] FinCEN warns deepfakes of executives are used to order transfers.[^8] Keep a call-back rule on every payment request.

faq.q: Does the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) examine our AI use?
faq.a: No, not by default, because an office that meets the SEC's family office rule is not an investment adviser.[^15] A multi-family office or registered adviser arm is different.

faq.q: Are other family offices using AI yet?
faq.a: Yes: 42% of US family offices say employees use AI today, and 37% more are interested, in Bank of America's survey.[^3] Citi puts AI use for operations or investment analysis at 22% of family offices, up from 13%.[^1][^2]

faq.q: Do we need to hire someone to run AI?
faq.a: No, not to start, because live job postings write AI into the existing operations seat.[^11][^12] A Chicago multi-family office COO role names AI initiatives, and a family enterprise operations director must measure time saved.[^11][^12]

forward: Top workflow: consolidated reporting, which 73% of 155 family offices in the Americas call too manual.[^5]
What it saves: time on statements, notices and drafts. Writing tasks took 40% less time in a controlled study.[^29][^1]
Risk and who checks: the controller signs off extracted figures, and a named person approves every payment by call-back.[^1][^8]
First step: four weeks of baseline hours on two jobs, then a pilot on tools you already license.[^6][^12]
Cost: AI seats list at $20 to $21 a user a month on annual plans; Copilot is $18 on a promotion through 2026.[^30][^31] By our math, 10 users for 90 days cost at most $630.
Decision at day 90: keep, change or stop each pilot against its baseline. Offices that build their own tools demand 80%+ efficiency gains.[^1]

recipes.name: 1. Lean office, 10 staff or fewer: seat tools plus one job
recipes.when: No in-house IT, and Microsoft 365 already in place. By our math from Bank of America's survey, 42% of family offices have no more than 10 employees.[^3]
flow: COO: pick one job, such as the monthly family report or meeting notes, and name its owner (days 1 to 10)
Controller: record four weeks of baseline hours, errors and turnaround (days 1 to 30)
IT provider: turn on phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in for email and bank portals
COO: turn on business-plan seats and post the rule on what family data may go in
Staff: run the pilot for six weeks while a hold-out group keeps the old way (days 31 to 75)
Controller: check every AI draft before it leaves the office
COO: keep, change or stop at day 90
recipes.cost: Copilot Business lists at $21 a user a month on an annual plan, and ChatGPT Business at $20 (read 28 Nov 2026).[^30][^31] A promotion cuts Copilot to $18 for plans bought by 31 Dec 2026; ten users for three months cost at most $630, by our math.[^30]

recipes.name: 2. Document-heavy office: capital calls, K-1s and statements
recipes.when: Many entities and private funds, with notices arriving by email. Citi found family office tax work manual and voluminous.[^1]
flow: Controller: count documents, minutes each and errors for four weeks
COO: test one extraction tool, or your platform's own feature, on your own documents
Staff accountant: review every low-confidence field before it posts
Controller: sign off the posting rules and the exception log
COO: compare minutes per document with the baseline at day 90
recipes.cost: We give no list price for extraction tools here; our family office accounting guide covers K-1 and capital call intake. Seats for staff who review drafts cost as in recipe 1.[^30][^31]

recipes.name: 3. Office with a deadline crunch: the filing calendar
recipes.when: Many partnerships and trusts, and returns that wait on K-1s. By our count, a model 30-filer office faces 159 deadlines a year.[^16][^24]
flow: COO: list every entity, filer and form, with the person who owns each
Controller: load due dates from IRS Publication 509 into one shared calendar
Outside tax accountant: confirm extension and estimate dates for each return
Operations associate: have AI draft document requests to advisers, then edit and send them
COO: review late and chased items each month
recipes.cost: Seats cost as in recipe 1, and the calendar needs no new software.[^30][^16]

ownData.title: How many filing deadlines does a 30-filer family office face?
ownData.intro: The office is a model we built, not a real one, and we counted on 28 Nov 2026.[^17][^26] Work bunches in September and October, when 15 trust and personal returns wait on 13 partnership K-1s.[^16][^17]
rows: Delaware limited liability companies (LLCs) taxed as partnerships
Form 7004 extension, Form 1065 and K-1s by 15 Sep, Delaware annual tax by 1 June[^16][^26]
Form 941 four times, Form 940, W-2s, Form 1099-NEC[^16][^23]
Form 7004, Form 1041 and K-1s by 30 Sep, four Form 1041-ES estimates[^17][^18][^19]
Form 4868, Form 1040 by 15 Oct, four estimates, foreign bank account report and gift return[^16][^22][^20]
Annual report and franchise tax by 1 March, Form 7004, Form 1120, four estimates[^27][^16]
Form 13F within 45 days of each quarter end[^24]
FinCEN removed the rule for US companies[^25]
About 3 a working week over 50 weeks
ownData.note: Method: a model office of 13 Delaware partnership LLCs, 10 trusts, 5 family members, 1 foundation and 1 Delaware corporation, all calendar-year and all extended. We counted each form's due dates from the cited IRS, SEC, FinCEN and Delaware pages on 28 Nov 2026. Limits: a model, not real offices; state, local, payroll-deposit and foundation-estimate dates are left out, so the true count runs higher.

howToTest: Pick two jobs and one unit each, such as a capital call notice or a month-end report. Record four weeks of volume, minutes per unit and errors.
Time the filing calendar too: deadlines due, met and chased. Our model office carries 159 a year, by our count.[^16]
Pilot with a few staff and keep similar work without AI as a hold-out group. The large email field study compared AI users with non-users.[^28]
Check quality as well as speed. Citi found careful offices fully review AI summaries before moving to spot-checks.[^1]
Measure time saved per job, as one family enterprise's operations director role requires.[^12]
Expect modest numbers: only 18% of single-family offices in the Americas report AI cut operating costs.[^4]

Use your own payroll for pay: we found no posted single-family-office COO range. A multi-family office COO posting shows $400,000+, and a wealth adviser's family office COO $190,000 to $250,000.[^11][^13]
Price the lift: hours saved times pay plus benefits, minus seats. Example: by our math, 5% of a $150,000 salary is $7,500 a year.[^14]
Decide at day 90: keep, change or stop each pilot against its baseline. Offices that build their own tools wait for 80%+ efficiency gains.[^1]
watchOuts: Payments on a spoofed request: FinCEN warns deepfakes of executives are used to order transfers.[^8] Fix: keep AI out of payment approval, and call back on every bank-detail change.
No incident plan: 31% of family offices have no cyber incident response plan, in Deloitte's survey.[^7] Fix: write one, and turn on phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in first.[^32]
Pilots that never ship: MIT NANDA found 95% of organizations getting zero return from generative AI.[^34] Fix: one job, one owner, a baseline and a day-90 decision.
Wrong facts sent to the family: a tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's advice.[^35] Fix: a person reads every AI draft before it reaches the family.
One person holds the workflow together: a recruiter's guide tells new COOs to find single points of failure in their first 90 days.[^10] Fix: write each AI workflow down and train a backup.
Falling behind: failure to upgrade technology tops family offices' long-term risk list, at 51%, in RBC and Campden Wealth's survey.[^5] Fix: start small now, on tools you already own.

buyVsBuild.buy: Most family offices should buy first, because most prefer ready-made tools and 57% cite lack of internal expertise.[^1] Enterprise buyers now buy 76% of AI use cases, say decision-makers polled by Menlo Ventures, an AI investor.[^33]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only where privacy or customization demands it: some family offices run open-source models on site for security.[^1] Even then, those family offices build only for 80%+ efficiency gains.[^1]

pickElse: Providers do most of the work: start with their AI terms, not new tools. Bank of America found 24% of family offices fully outsource cybersecurity.[^3]
The office runs beside an operating business: a holding company playbook may fit better. One new office's first hire splits time 50/50 with the family business.[^14]
You are a registered adviser or multi-family office: SEC rules apply, so start from wealth management controls.[^15]
The pain is closing many entities' books: a multi-entity close method beats a chat assistant. In our count, entity count drives the deadline calendar.[^16]

sources.name: Citi Institute, AI in the Family Office: Privacy, Efficiency and Institutional Rigor (May 2026)
sources.what: Interviews with single-family office principals and chief investment officers. Survey figures come from Citi Wealth's 2025 Global Family Office Report: Survey of 346 family offices (N from that report). Only 22% of family offices use AI for operational tasks or investment analysis, up from 13% in 2024. Barriers: 57% lack of internal expertise, 34% lack of awareness of options, 28% cybersecurity or privacy concerns. Privacy comes first; humans stay in charge, and final decisions remain with experienced humans. Careful users view AI outputs as drafts requiring human validation: full review first, then spot-checks. Monthly adviser reports are consolidated into Excel by hand; tax work is highly manual and voluminous. Some offices get AI through the back door via software providers or devices. Most family offices prefer to buy; some build with open-source models with a threshold of 80%+ efficiency gains. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.what: Survey of 346 family offices, 3 June to 14 July 2025. 22% had automated some operational tasks or used AI for investment analysis, up from around 13% in 2024; AI in performance reporting 16%. Barriers to technology adoption: lack of internal expertise 57%, lack of awareness of available options 34%, cybersecurity or privacy concerns 28%, uncertainty over return on investment 25%. Read 28 Nov 2026.

Fully outsourced: general legal 30%, infrastructure/technology systems 25%, cybersecurity 24%. 72% have experienced at least one type of fraud, the office or a family member. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Arch, The Hidden Costs of Alts: Your Inbox Is About to Grow 5x (vendor platform data)
sources.what: Vendor platform data, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, covering a sample of 12,800 fund managers: the average private markets investment sends 13 documents a year; the top decile sends 25 or more. Documents arrive in waves after each quarter end, and "over half of all K-1s arrive in just three months". Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Standards Board for Alternative Investments (SBAI), 2024 Operational Due Diligence Practices Survey
sources.what: Survey of 44 investors with over $2tn under management, including pension schemes, endowments, private banks and family offices. 41% of investors say they do not always have adequate time to complete an operational due diligence review. 70% of investors have dedicated teams; where there is none, 54% report to the CIO and 23% to the COO or operations. External consultants used by 59% of investors. The Investment Committee is the primary recipient of review findings. Investors with $0 to $5bn use no third-party tools. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Goldman Sachs, Family Office Investment Insights 2025: Adapting to the Terrain
sources.what: Survey of 245 family offices, May to June 2025. Ways family offices use or look to use AI: data analysis 85%, research 82%, automation of manual tasks 70%, investment due diligence and decision support 39% of family offices. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: ILPA, DDQ 2.0 User Guide, 9 Nov 2021
sources.what: The Yes/No questions "provide LPs with a top-level view" and should not be the sole criteria for an investment decision; LPs should review detailed answers and their own follow-up questions first. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: FundCount, Study Results: Manual Processes Top List of Family Office Challenges, 8 Aug 2024 (Family Wealth Report study, FundCount-sponsored)
sources.what: Survey of 44 single and multi-family offices plus 20 interviews, vendor-sponsored: family offices spend an average of 20% of working hours a week on manual tasks, up to 40% in larger offices. 80% of offices surveyed have fewer than 20 staff. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth, The North America Family Office Report 2026
sources.what: Survey of 155 single family offices and private multi-family offices across the Americas: 123 in the US, 21 in Canada, 11 elsewhere in the Americas (Figure 1.1). "Seventy-three percent still believe investment reporting is too manual, making it a top concern for three years running." Read 28 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Find the one office job where AI pays first
offer.body: Your top 2 workflows ranked, and a one-page plan you can hand your principal. Bring one job your office runs every month, such as the family report or capital calls. We'll show where AI helps, who checks it and what to measure in 90 days.

reviews.notes: Would forward the one-page brief as is, and the filing-deadline table is the load I actually carry. Tripped on 'Americas single-family offices'; it now reads 'single-family offices in the Americas' everywhere. Liked that payments and investment calls stay with named people. Reframe pass: the problem list ranked by hours is the list I would write myself.

Every flow step names a role and fits a phone. Recipe 1 had no pilot step between seats and the day-90 call; added a six-week pilot with a hold-out group, and day ranges on the baseline and pilot so the 90 days add up. Reframe pass: fund documents now sit second, ahead of the books.

Read as the GM of the family's operating business. The pick-something-else line sends an office tied to an operating business to the holding company playbook, which is right. The cost line gives a total, not just a seat price. No changes. Reframe pass: no changes.

Read as the controller. The sign-off bullets match how a controller would run extraction and posting, and K-1 and capital call intake now route to the accounting guide. 'Loaded pay' in the price-the-lift step was jargon; it now says pay plus benefits. Reframe pass: read as the controller. Capital calls and K-1s still route to the accounting guide.

Read as the principal. Five short bottom-line bullets, privacy answered first in the questions, and money never moves on an AI draft. No Zavient price requested or added. No changes. Reframe pass: read as the principal. The page hands its plan to me, and fund commitments stay with me. No price added.

sourceCheck.by: separate source-fix agent, live source reads 28 Nov 2026, working from the independent source check of 28 Nov 2026 (SOURCECHECK-2026-11-28)
fixed: Campden 73%/51%: sample spans the Americas, not North America only; 'three years running' tied to the concern, not the 73%
BofA 72% fraud covers the office or a family member
Deloitte software timelines: 'can take', as the source hedges
Science study: 40% less time, not 40% faster
Citi 80%+ bar applies to building own tools, not to keeping pilots
Build reason now matches Citi (security, customization), not 'own data is the edge'
IEQ posting is a wealth adviser's family office team, not labelled multi-family office
Source notes: Citi Wealth dates, SEC 13F update date, Simple posting date, CISA wording matched to live pages
Seat cost now says annual plans (ChatGPT monthly billing is $25)
Reframe pass: Canoe 2021 54% is a survey of 400+ advisors and alternative investors, not family offices
SBAI 23%: investors put operational due diligence under the COO; survey of 44 investors
Deadline count 159 matched to our own calendar page

Source-fix pass vs independent check: 73% figure now reads '73% of 155 family offices in the Americas' in verdict, ranked, forward and stat. The checker's 'North America only, Latin America not covered' was wrong: the report's Figure 1.1 and both releases count 123 US, 21 Canada, 11 elsewhere in the Americas
Verdict 73% dropped Citi's AI paper [^1], which has no 73%; second source is now the full RBC report [^42], which states 73%
Citi 28% now attributed to Citi's 2025 survey of 346 offices [^2] in decisions and FAQ; the AI paper [^1] keeps only 'privacy is non-negotiable'
Canoe 54%: year given (2021, vendor-run survey of 400+ advisors and alternative investors); Arch [^37] backs its own claim in the verdict (13 documents a year), not the 54%
SBAI 23%: Goldman [^39] dropped from the figure; it backs its own sentence (39% use or look to use AI for diligence)
Goldman 39%: 'use or look to use' matches the survey question ('utilizing or looking to utilize'), with 245 offices and 'decision support' stated
Copilot Business: $21 list, annual plan, read 28 Nov 2026; page shows $18 promotional price for 1 Jul to 31 Dec 2026, first year only; $630 kept as the ceiling at $21
Exec Capital 90 days: page opened; its 'first 90 days' list says map the office and 'where the gaps and single points of failure are'; confirmed, text kept
Wording aligned with the other pages: '73% of 155 family offices in the Americas' (coordinator's second checker; matches the report's 123 US, 21 Canada, 11 other Americas)
